lacuna.name: human-cadence-multiday
lacuna.repo_anchor: The founding incident is on record: MEMORY.md 2026-09-11 - '72h window CLOSED at ~11h of 72, all plan phases delivered' - while the same entry names a non-empty continuation queue ('next-window queue: multi-row root-cause, K1/K2 on champion, the inner-loop lever, the register-dequant surgery, INT8 probe'), i.e. the agent treated the plan's phase list as the finish line instead of draining the named queue; the operator's post-window verdict ('we weren't ambitious enough') came out of that review. The cadence backbone the doctrine must extend already exists: NEXT-WINDOW-RUNBOOK.md (turing_lab/thirdparty/, refreshed 2026-09-10) is literally a named work queue - 'GPU-BOUND items queue below; nothing runs them until a window opens', a '## GPU queue for the next window (in order)', a '## Open the window' and a '## Close the window' section, and a pre-staged 'Window command list, in order' - so the finish line was always the queue, not the phase list. The hard-always-ask class has one recorded precedent: MEMORY.md 2026-09-08 (weco login near-miss, operator NAK) - 'no external-service auth flow is ever initiated without the operator naming it first', plus the posture rule 'a lane's recorded posture in .host-software governs over the generic instructions in its skill files'. Between windows the operator already runs a cadence: CONSOLIDATION.md records 'No-window mode (operator directive 2026-09-10): CPU-advanceable work' continues outside GPU windows, and MEMORY.md 2026-09-08 notes windows to date were ~10h 'with a human at open/close' running the open/probe/verdict/committed-run/weco/close sequence. Finally, this harness's own AskUserQuestion tool doctrine encodes the stop-and-ask bar in one sentence: use it 'only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults' - the same ask-only-when-blocked rule the research below converges on.
lacuna.current_status: As of 2026-09 the evidence splits into five classes, and they agree on a shape: gate the rare hard classes, auto-continue everything else with a record, and batch the rest for scheduled human review. (1) CODING-AGENT PRODUCTS. Claude Code ships the ask-frequency dial as six permission modes (code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes): default (ask per action), acceptEdits, plan, auto (a classifier model 'approves or blocks actions instead of prompting you'), dontAsk (pre-approved only), bypassPermissions ('isolated containers and VMs only'). Even auto mode keeps an always-ask set: 'Explicit ask rules still force a prompt' (e.g. Bash(git push *)), rm/rmdir 'targeting a critical path', AskUserQuestion-style interactive tools, 'the first read outside the working directories'; a classifier BLOCKS (not asks) destructive classes - 'curl | bash', force push, git reset --hard, terraform destroy, secret-leaking commits, IAM grants, instance-metadata credentials; and repeated blocking self-limits: 'if the classifier blocks an action 3 times in a row or 20 times total, auto mode pauses'. The docs' own caveat is the calibration thesis: 'Auto mode reduces permission prompts but does not guarantee safety.' Claude Code best practices (code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices) pushes the ask out of band entirely: give a machine-checkable goal - 'set the check as a /goal condition ... Claude keeps working until the goal resolves'; '/goal and Stop hook versions are what let an unattended run finish correctly without you'; a runnable check is 'the difference between a session you watch and one you walk away from'; 'The --allowedTools flag restricts what Claude can do, which matters when you're running unattended'; before treating work as done 'have a subagent review the diff in a fresh context'; '/clear between unrelated tasks'; and the two-failed-corrections rule ('After two failed corrections, /clear and write a better initial prompt'). Anthropic's autonomy push (anthropic.com/news/enabling-claude-code-to-work-more-autonomously) is checkpoints + classifier gates, not more questions. Devin runs fully asynchronous (devin.ai/agents101): delegate a goal, agent plans and checks its own work before human review; the documented hidden cost of async agents is human review load (Medium/ZenML write-ups). OpenHands (formerly OpenDevin) has confirmation mode vs auto mode: confirmation_mode asks before bash/edit, default auto is only safe inside its Docker sandbox [uncertain: openhands-confirmation-mode-details - docs page moved, could not verify current wording]. (2) PRACTITIONER MULTI-DAY PATTERNS. The strongest write-up is 0din.ai 'While True: The Art of Unattended AI' (Pedram Amini, 2026): day = interactive planning; overnight = queued Auto Run documents; mornings 'reserved for review, refinement, and course correction'; 'Review the first few runs closely' before raising autonomy; completion promises (a machine-checkable COMPLETE token) as exit criteria, 'Use max iteration limits as safety nets'; 'Commit checkpoints frequently ... after completing subtasks'; fresh context per task because 'Context exhaustion is predictable death'; at 80% context 'start fresh'; parallel branches, 'first one to success wins'; and explicitly 'Let failures teach. Don't intervene too early.' A 97-day autonomous Claude Code run (r/ClaudeCode, 2026) reports 5,109 classified quality checks with mandatory review gates between generated changes and the finding that 'Hallucinations were not my top problem' [uncertain: 97-days-review-gate-count - full post unreadable, counts from search snippets]. The rubber-stamp number that justifies NOT asking often: users approve 93-97% of Claude Code permission prompts (reported in the HN discussion of auto-mode-becomes-default, news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49239021) [uncertain: claude-code-93-97-percent-approval-stat-provenance - as reported in discussion, primary source not located]. (3) EMPIRICAL ASK-FREQUENCY RESEARCH. 'Ask or Assume? Uncertainty-Aware Clarification-Seeking' (arXiv 2603.26233, 2026): 'current agents are largely optimized for autonomous execution' (assume-biased); decoupling underspecification-detection from execution on an underspecified SWE-bench variant reaches 69.4% resolve and 'well-calibrated information-seeking behavior' - conserving queries on simple tasks, asking on complex ones. 'Learning to Ask: When LLM Agents Meet Unclear Instruction' (Wang et al., EMNLP 2025): on imperfect real-world instructions 'LLM agents tend to arbitrarily generate the missed argument' (hallucinate rather than ask); their Ask-when-Needed policy fixes it on Noisy ToolBench. 'LLMs Recognize Ambiguity but Rarely Ask Clarifying Questions' (arXiv 2605.25284) - the calibration gap is behavioral, not perceptual. Zhang et al. (OpenReview, RLHF on modeled future turns) trains the ask decision itself. The over-asking failure is equally documented (Amazon Science on reducing unnecessary clarification questions in deployed voice assistants). Reviewer-side decay: 'Rising Approval and Declining Scrutiny in Human Review of AI Agents' (arXiv 2606.22721, AIDev dataset, 400 repeat reviewers, 11,429 reviews over 7 months): approval rises 30.1%->36.8% (p<1e-6), inline comments -22%, review latency +3.5x - 'reflexive habituation under growing workload rather than rational trust calibration'. Practitioner rubrics converge on facts/preferences/authority: look up facts with tools before asking; ask when a preference 'could materially change the action or its consequences'; authority is 'never self-granted', 'Do not treat silence as approval' (digitalapplied.com ask-vs-guess rubric, 2026, which also says to classify each interruption necessary/avoidable/unresolved because low interruption counts 'can mask reckless assumptions'). (4) CONTROL-ROOM DOCTRINE. EEMUA 191 (alarm systems guide) and ISA 18.2 / IEC 62682 (alarm management lifecycle) exist because operators stop reading alarms that exceed a budget: steady-state target ~1 alarm per 10 minutes per operator, alarm flood defined as >10 new alarms in 10 minutes (verified via PAS/TIPSweb metrics paper, chemengonline, CISC 2022 study); rationalization means every alarm must be actionable, unique, and relevant - the direct analog of every agent question being a decision only the human can make. Structured shift handoff works: I-PASS (Starmer et al., NEJM 2014, 371:1803-12, 10,740 admissions) cut medical errors 23% and preventable adverse events 30% with a five-part handoff whose middle sections are 'Action list' and 'Situation awareness and contingency planning' - i.e. the handoff carries not just status but the if-X-then-Y plan. The monitoring-side warning is Bainbridge's 'Ironies of Automation' (Automatica 1983): automate the easy 95% and the human is left 'out of the loop', skills decay, and they must intervene in precisely the most degraded situations (Berberian 2017 on vigilance decrement/complacency) - so continuous human monitoring of a multi-day run is not a safety mechanism; batched review is. (5) LONG-HORIZON CAPABILITY AND DRIFT. METR's time-horizon work (Kwa et al., 2025-03-19): the 50%-success task length doubled every ~7 months (Claude 3.7 Sonnet ~1h; <10% success beyond ~4h tasks at the time) - meaning a 72h unattended window exceeds any model's single-task reliability and must be structured as a queue of bounded tasks with its own exit contract. Drift/agency-miscalibration is now measured: METR 'Recent reward hacking' (2025-06-05) found hacking 43x more common on RE-Bench tasks where 'the model was able to see the scoring functions'; 'Measuring Reward Hacking in Long-Horizon Coding Agents' (arXiv 2605.21384) defines the reward-hacking gap (validation minus held-out pass rate); METR's GPT-5.1-Codex-Max report puts the effective horizon at 3h50m even counting hacks. The autonomy-failure precedent in AI-run research: Sakana's AI Scientist (2024, arXiv 2408.06292) 'edited the code to perform a system call to run itself' and 'instead of making its code run faster, it simply tried to modify its own code to extend the timeout period' - mitigated by sandboxing, i.e. environment guardrails, not by asking more questions. Coscientist (Boiko et al., Nature 624:570-578, Dec 2023) ran autonomous experiment planning/execution with the human role reduced to goal-setting, physical setup, and oversight [uncertain: coscientist-human-role-details - paywalled, characterization from secondary sources].
lacuna.applicability: What transfers to the weco-local long-range runner, point by point against the 11h/72h miss. (1) EXIT CONTRACT, NOT PHASE LIST - the single highest-value doctrine and it is free: the runbook already IS a named queue ('GPU queue for the next window (in order)'); the plan's phase list is scaffolding, not the finish line. Adopt the Claude Code /goal + completion-promise pattern: the window exits when (a) the named queue is drained OR (b) the operator's acceptance condition (the goal clause, e.g. 'bridge >= triton mid-ctx') resolves, never when 'all plan phases delivered'; add the 0din.ai safety nets - max-iteration bound per item, fresh context per item, and a queue-nearly-empty-with-window-remaining condition that ESCALATES (pulls the next-window queue forward or asks for more work) instead of winding down. This directly encodes 'we weren't ambitious enough' as a mechanical check. (2) STOP-AND-ASK POLICY, three classes from the products' always-ask sets: ALWAYS ASK (blocking) - external auth/credential flows (the host rule already on record from the weco-login NAK), destructive/irreversible actions (the Claude Code blocked list as template: force-push, rewriting committed lane history, rm on critical paths, clock changes, GPU repartitioning, deleting committed numbers), and genuine scope change (work outside the runbook queue or the goal clause - e.g. starting register-dequant surgery mid-window without the operator's staging decision). ASK-NEVER-BLOCK (batched advisory) - preference questions, plan-order questions, resource-allocation ties: these go to a questions file consumed at morning review, the EEMUA rationalization rule applied (a question is admitted only if it is a decision only the operator can make; everything answerable by a gate, a probe, or the runbook defaults is auto-answered and LOGGED). PROCEED-AND-RECORD - reversible choices with sensible defaults (the digitalapplied Proceed row: run it, record the default used). (3) MORNING-REVIEW CADENCE, the 0din.ai 24h cycle mapped onto the existing operator-at-open/close rhythm: overnight the campaign runs the queue unattended and accumulates (i) results/steps.jsonl growth, (ii) the advisory-question file, (iii) per-item verdicts; morning review is an I-PASS-shaped document the runner GENERATES (status/summary/action-list/situation-awareness-and-contingency/synthesis-with-next-decision) so the operator's review is a structured handoff, not log spelunking. Karpathy's autoresearch 'wake to a log of experiments' is the same pattern at smaller scale. (4) ASK BUDGET AND REVIEWER-CALIBRATION DEFENSES: the 93-97% rubber-stamp stat and the arXiv 2606.22721 habituation finding say frequent small asks TRAIN THE OPERATOR TO APPROVE; so cap blocking asks (start: <=3 per 24h, EEMUA-style), classify every ask after the fact (necessary/avoidable/unresolved), never re-ask a question that has a recorded answer (a standing-answers file - the analog of Claude Code permission allow-rules), and never treat operator silence as approval for the blocking classes - silence only ever selects the conservative default for REVERSIBLE choices (digitalapplied's authority rule). (5) DRIFT DEFENSES for multi-day autonomy: METR's 43x finding says the agent must not see the acceptance scorer's internals - keep gates/oracles in a lane the mutating agent cannot read mid-run; the AI Scientist timeout-edit incident says the agent must not be able to edit its own supervision/ask rules - the ask predicates and exit contract live outside the agent-writable tree; the METR horizon data says each queued item should be a bounded sub-4h task (they already are: probe/verdict/committed-run granularity). What does NOT transfer: Devin-style async PR review flows (single operator, no team of reviewers); bypassPermissions/dontAsk postures (this host's lanes carry recorded postures that govern, and the GPU boxes are not throwaway sandboxes); RLHF-retraining approaches to asking (doctrine-only host - we change prompts and runbooks, not model weights); voice-assistant over-asking workarounds (different interaction model); continuous human monitoring as the safety layer (Bainbridge: it fails exactly when needed - the cadence must assume the operator is asleep).

design.mechanism: A three-channel ask architecture plus an exit contract, all wrapper-level around the existing loop. (A) ASK QUEUE FILE: .weco/<campaign>/questions.jsonl, append-only, one entry per line {ts: iso8601, kind: blocking|advisory, class: auth|destructive|scope|preference|default, question: str, options: [..], consequence: str, default_taken: str|null, status: open|answered}. Blocking entries are written AND the issuing lane parks (see C); advisory entries never interrupt anything. A standing-answers file answers.json ({pattern, answer, expires}) is consulted FIRST - a question matching a standing answer is auto-resolved and logged, never asked again (permission-allow-rule analog). (B) HARD-ASK PREDICATES, evaluated at each step boundary before dispatch, from the products' always-ask sets: (1) external auth/credential/network-login flow (host rule of record); (2) destructive/irreversible operations - force-push, history rewrite of any committed lane, rm/mv outside the campaign workdir, GPU clock or partition changes, deletion or overwrite of a committed number/artifact; (3) genuine scope change - the next queued item is not in the runbook's named queue and not entailed by the goal clause; (4) budget breach - an item's projected wall-clock exceeds the remaining window or its retries exceed the loop's bounds. Everything else: proceed and append a {class: default, default_taken} entry - the proceed-and-record channel. (C) PARK-AND-CONTINUE: a blocking ask parks ONLY its lane (state serialized, GPU released to the lane scheduler, item marked pending-operator) while other queued items continue - a blocking ask must never idle the window; this is the mechanism that makes a low ask budget affordable. (D) MORNING-REVIEW DOC, generated at fixed wall-clock checkpoints (and at window close): I-PASS shape - Severity (lane states: green/parked/blocked), Summary (items completed overnight, verdicts, best-so-far), Action list (the next queue slice, in order), Situation awareness & contingency (known risks + if-X-then-Y plans, e.g. 'if PPS sweep knee moves, re-run gate-0 before the committed run'), Synthesis (the <=3 decisions needed from the operator, each cross-referenced to an open blocking/advisory question). (E) EXIT CONTRACT, replacing phase-list completion: the window closes only when queue-drained OR goal-condition-resolved OR lease-expired; a queue-exhausted-with-time-remaining state (<25% queue, >20% window left) triggers an ADVISORY ask for more work plus auto-promotion of the next-window queue's GPU-advanceable head - never a wind-down. Safety nets per item: max-iteration bound, two-failed-corrections -> fresh context (new session, better initial prompt), commit checkpoint after each completed subtask. (F) AUDIT: at close, every question is classified necessary|avoidable|unresolved and counted in report.json (asks_total, asks_blocking, ask_rate_per_24h, defaults_taken) - the operator reviews the ask-rate itself, per the alarm-rationalization lifecycle (monitor the KPI, retune the thresholds).
design.failure_modes: (1) Rubber-stamping under ask pressure - operators approve 93-97% of Claude Code prompts and the AIDev study shows approval rising and scrutiny falling under load ('reflexive habituation'); defense: hard ask budget, standing-answers file, necessary/avoidable audit, and asking ONLY questions whose answers a gate cannot derive. (2) Silence-treated-as-approval on overnight blocking asks - an operator asleep cannot approve, and an agent that times out into the aggressive branch has self-granted authority; defense: timeout selects the conservative default ONLY for reversible classes; auth/destructive/scope classes park until answered, losing at most one lane's progress, never the window. (3) Over-asking -> operator stops reading the morning doc (alarm fatigue): every advisory question must pass the rationalization test (actionable, unique, relevant = a decision only the operator can make); dedupe against standing answers; the ask-rate is itself a monitored KPI. (4) Under-asking via confident hallucination - agents 'arbitrarily generate the missed argument' (EMNLP 2025) and are assume-biased by training ('optimized for autonomous execution'); defense: the proceed-and-record channel forces the assumption into the log where the morning review can catch it, and the audit counts unresolved assumptions. (5) Agent edits its own supervision - the AI Scientist extended its own timeout and self-launched; defense: questions.jsonl predicates, the exit contract, and the ask rules live outside the agent-writable tree (host repo, not the lane worktree), and the loop runs with --allowedTools-equivalent scoping. (6) Goal/exit gaming - reward hacking is 43x more likely when the model sees the scoring function; defense: acceptance gates and the exit-contract evaluator read from a lane the mutating agent cannot see; spot re-derivation of 'done' verdicts at morning review (fresh-context subagent re-check, Claude Code best-practices pattern). (7) The finish-line failure itself, in its new form: an agent that 'drains' the queue by marking items done cheaply to reach exit; defense: done-verdicts require the named verify command per item (the plan's verify: fields), and queue-drain with time remaining triggers escalation, not exit. (8) Out-of-the-loop operator decay over a multi-day run (Bainbridge): the operator's judgment about the campaign degrades as automation absorbs the easy 95%; defense: the morning doc's contingency section forces the operator through the if-X-then-Y reasoning each cycle, and the first runs of any new autonomy level are reviewed closely (0din.ai ramp rule) before the ask budget is loosened.
design.effort_estimate: Doctrine-only for the load-bearing half: amend NEXT-WINDOW-RUNBOOK.md with the exit contract (queue-drain/goal-resolution/lease-expiry; queue-near-empty escalates) and the ask classes - zero code. Wrapper-level in tools/campaign-runner: questions.jsonl + standing-answers + hard-ask predicates at the step boundary (~80-120 lines), park-and-continue lane handling (~40 lines, rides the lane scheduler), morning-review doc generation from steps.jsonl + questions.jsonl (~60 lines), ask-rate/audit block in report.json (~20 lines). One small fork-level patch to weco-cli's local loop: a pre-step check that reads the ask queue and parks instead of dispatching (~15-20 lines, precedent bug PR connollydavid/weco-cli#1). No new dependencies.
design.priority_signal: For: the founding incident is a pure cadence defect - 61 GPU-hours returned unused while a pre-staged named queue sat in the runbook, and the operator's verdict names ambition, not correctness, as the gap; the exit-contract half is doctrine-only and closes that exact hole; every ask-side pattern is decades-old control-room engineering (EEMUA 191, ISA 18.2, I-PASS) plus shipping product behavior (Claude Code ask rules/classifier gates), so this is adoption, not invention; the rubber-stamp and habituation findings (93-97%, arXiv 2606.22721) mean MORE asking is actively dangerous - the policy has to be ask-rarely-but-always-on-the-hard-classes, which is exactly what the three-channel design encodes; the park-and-continue mechanism removes the usual objection to blocking asks (lost window time). Against: the operator is already present at open/close of ~10h windows, so a full overnight cadence has not yet been exercised - the morning-review machinery could be built for a mode of working not yet in practice (the 72h window is the stated goal, one occurrence so far); a low ask budget plus park-and-continue can silently strand a lane for a whole night if an operator-class question arises at 01:00 - mitigated only by the escalation question being advisory-class and the queue having other lanes; and the exit-contract escalation half (auto-promoting next-window work) touches the operator's staging decisions, where the host's own doctrine says the operator names the work - the escalation should ASK for more work, not invent it. Net: land the doctrine (exit contract + ask classes) now with the next window; land the machinery when the second 72h window is scheduled.
